spans.s:
Śiśu Āṅgirasa (‘descendant of aṅgiras’) is the name of the seer of a sāman or Chant in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes xiii. 3, 24. Cf. Hillebrandt, Vedische Mythologie, 2, 160.

Śiśuka in the Atharvaveda seems to be an adjective meaning ‘young,’ but according to Bloomfield it has the sense of ‘foal.’ The commentator, Sāyaṇa, reads śuśuka, which he explains as a ‘wild animal so called.’ Cf. āśuṃga.
Foot notes vi. 14, 3. Cf. Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 291.
Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 464.
2. Śiśumāra is a term applied to Śarkara in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa (xiv. 5, 15), where he is called a Śiśumārarṣi, explained by the commentator to mean a ṛṣi in the form of a Siśumāra.

Siśna-deva, occurring twice in the Rigveda in the plural, means ‘those who have the phallus for a deity.’ The term most probably refers to the phallus worship of the aborigines.
Foot notes vii. 21, 5; x. 99, 3. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 118; Hopkins, Religions of India, 150; von Schroeder, Vienna Oriental Journal, 9, 237; Macdonell, Vedic Mythology, 155; Keith, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1911, 1002, n. 5.

Śīṣṭa occurs only in a vālakhilya hymn of the Rigveda, where the word seems to be the name of an unimportant clan.
Foot notes viii. 53, 4. Cf. Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 163.

Sīsa, ‘lead,’ occurs first in the Atharvaveda, where it is mentioned as used for amulets. The word is then quite common. The use of lead by the weaver as a weight is perhaps also referred to.
Foot notes xii. 2, 1. 19 et seq., 53.
i. 16, 2, 4.
Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 4, 2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xviii. 13; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, iii. 12, 6, 5; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, v. 1, 2, 14; 4, 1, 9; xii. 7, 1, 7; 2, 10; Chāndogya upaniṣad, iv. 17, 7, etc.
Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 80; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 11, 9; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 4. This is the view of Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v., and of Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 53. But Griffith, Translation of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, 183, n., thinks that in xix. 80 lead is referred to not as a weight, but as a charm against demons and sorcery.
Cf. Bloomfield, Journal of the American Oriental Society, 15, 157, 158.
